items.front: What is value in ITIL?
items.back: The perceived benefits, usefulness and importance of something. The stakeholder judges it, not the provider, and it is more than money.

items.front: What is a product in ITIL?
items.back: A configuration of an organization's resources, such as people, information, technology, partners and money, designed to offer value for a consumer.

items.front: Which two things does a service take off the customer's hands?
items.back: Specific costs and risks. The service facilitates the outcomes the customer wants without the customer having to manage them.

items.front: Utility in three words?
items.back: Fit for purpose: what the product or service does. It supports a performance or removes a constraint.

items.front: Warranty in three words?
items.back: Fit for use: how well it does it against agreed requirements, covering availability, capacity, security and continuity.

items.front: Can one person be customer, user and sponsor at the same time?
items.back: Yes. The three roles are distinct, but one person or group can hold several of them at once.

items.front: What three parts make up a service relationship?
items.back: Service provision, service consumption and service relationship management.

items.front: What is a service offering?
items.back: A description of one or more services, designed for a target consumer group. It can include goods, access to resources and service actions.

items.front: Who creates value, in ITIL's view?
items.back: Providers, consumers and other stakeholders together, through active collaboration. A provider does not hand value to a passive consumer.

items.front: What five factors are weighed in value co-creation in Version 5?
items.back: Outcomes, costs, risks, experience and sustainability.

items.front: What is experience, as a value factor?
items.back: How a stakeholder perceives every contact with a product or service: ease, speed, clarity and trust. It shapes value even when targets are met.

items.front: What does sustainability mean when weighing value?
items.back: Whether the value can last, and what producing it costs over time in energy, hardware, workload and future money.

items.front: What is the watermelon effect (a common term, not an ITIL exam term)?
items.back: Reports are green on every target while users are unhappy. Targets alone do not prove value, so experience must be measured too.

items.front: Which kind of experience does PeopleCert call a core focus of Version 5?
items.back: Digital experience: the quality of people's contact with digital products and services.

items.front: What does AI-native mean for ITIL Version 5?
items.back: It was designed with AI in mind from the start, so practices, value streams and roles can include AI to automate work and support decisions.

items.front: Who counts as a stakeholder in a service?
items.back: Anyone with an interest in it: customers, users, sponsors, employees, partners and suppliers, funders and society.

items.front: Which dimension covers skills, culture and resistance to change?
items.back: Organizations and People.

items.front: Which dimension covers information, knowledge and the technology that manages it, which can include AI?
items.back: Information and Technology.

items.front: Which dimension covers the steps and controls that turn demand into value?
items.back: Value Streams and Processes.

items.front: A new privacy law affects a service. Is that one of the four dimensions?
items.back: No. It is an outside factor that the dimensions must respond to. ITIL 4 grouped these as political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental; for Version 5, treat that list as background.

items.front: What is governance?
items.back: The means by which an organization is directed and controlled.

items.front: What three things does a governing body do?
items.back: Evaluate, direct and monitor, in the ITIL 4 model that Version 5 builds on. Management then runs the work within that direction.

items.front: A monthly review of improvement ideas belongs to which Value System component?
items.back: Continual improvement.

items.front: What are the inputs to the Value System in ITIL 4?
items.back: Opportunity and demand. Opportunity is an option to add value or improve; demand is the need for products and services.

items.front: When does a guiding principle apply?
items.back: In all circumstances, whatever the organization's goals, strategy, type of work or management structure.

items.front: Which principle says to know the consumer and how they experience the service?
items.back: Focus on value.

items.front: Under Start where you are, what should a decision to replace something rest on?
items.back: Evidence from observing and measuring what exists now, so what works can be reused.

items.front: Which principle says to break work into smaller pieces that each deliver value?
items.back: Progress iteratively with feedback.

items.front: Which principle says to make work, decisions and problems visible?
items.back: Collaborate and promote visibility.

items.front: Which principle says no service or component stands alone?
items.back: Think and work holistically. Work end to end and use all four dimensions.

items.front: Which principle removes a measure that nobody uses to decide anything?
items.back: Keep it simple and practical.

items.front: Do the guiding principles work one at a time?
items.back: No. They interact and several usually apply. In a question, pick the one the key words point to.

items.front: What does the Discover activity do?
items.back: Understands needs, demand and opportunities, and decides what is worth doing. (Our plain-word reading, not an official definition.)

items.front: What does the Design activity do?
items.back: Shapes the product or service, including how it will be used, supported and secured. (Our plain-word reading, not an official definition.)

items.front: What does the Acquire activity do?
items.back: Obtains the resources needed, from inside the organization or from partners and suppliers. (Our plain-word reading, not an official definition.)

items.front: What does the Build activity do?
items.back: Creates, configures and tests the components, using the resources acquired. (Our plain-word reading, not an official definition.)

items.front: Operate versus Deliver?
items.back: Operate keeps live technology and components running as agreed. Deliver provides the service to consumers. (Our plain-word reading, not an official definition.)

items.front: What does the Support activity do?
items.back: Helps users and restores normal use when things go wrong. (Our plain-word reading, not an official definition.)

items.front: Does every value stream use all eight lifecycle activities?
items.back: No. A value stream draws on the activities its demand needs, so it does not have to touch all eight.

items.front: What is technical debt?
items.back: The future cost of quick choices made now, such as a shortcut in Build that Operate and Support must pay for later.

items.front: How many management practices does Version 5 have, and in which groups?
items.back: 34, in two groups: Product and Service management practices, and General management practices.

items.front: What does the service desk practice do?
items.back: It captures demand for incident resolution and service requests, and is the single point of contact between the provider and all its users.

items.front: What is an incident?
items.back: An unplanned interruption to a service, or a reduction in its quality.

items.front: What two things set an incident's priority?
items.back: Impact and urgency.

items.front: What is a major incident?
items.back: An incident with significant business impact. It gets its own procedure: a clear lead, faster communication and more people.

items.front: What is a problem?
items.back: A cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents.

items.front: What are the three phases of problem management?
items.back: Problem identification, problem control and error control.

items.front: What are the three kinds of event?
items.back: Informational, warning and exception.

items.front: What does change enablement aim for?
items.back: To maximize the number of successful changes by assessing risk, authorizing changes and managing the change schedule.

items.front: What is a standard change?
items.back: A low-risk, well-understood change that is pre-authorized and done by a documented procedure, without fresh authorization each time.

items.front: What is a normal change?
items.back: A change that is assessed and authorized by the right change authority before it is made.

items.front: What is an emergency change?
items.back: A change that must be made as soon as possible, such as to stop a security threat, with faster assessment and authorization.

items.front: Who authorizes a change?
items.back: A change authority. It sits closer to the work for low-risk changes and higher up for high-risk ones.

items.front: Can a component be deployed before it is released?
items.back: Yes. Deployment moves it to the live environment; release makes it available for use, which can happen later.

items.front: What is a configuration item (CI)?
items.back: Any component that needs to be managed in order to deliver an IT service.

items.front: What is an IT asset?
items.back: Any financially valuable component that can contribute to delivering an IT product or service.

items.front: A vendor misses its contracted response time. Which practice handles it?
items.back: Supplier management: it monitors supplier performance against the contract and acts on it.

items.front: Is continual improvement a Value System component or a practice?
items.back: Both. It is a component of the ITIL Value System and one of the 34 management practices.

items.front: Who is responsible for continual improvement?
items.back: Everyone in the organization, at every level.

items.front: What is a continual improvement register (CIR)?
items.back: A record of improvement ideas with expected value, size, owner and status, used to do the most useful ideas first.

items.front: Continual improvement model: what are the first four steps?
items.back: What is the vision? Where are we now? Where do we want to be? How do we get there?

items.front: Continual improvement model: what are the last three steps?
items.back: Take action. Did we get there? How do we keep the momentum going?

items.front: What is lead time in a value stream?
items.back: The total time from trigger to value: all work time plus all wait time.

items.front: How is flow efficiency calculated?
items.back: Total work time divided by lead time, a standard value stream mapping measure. A low figure means items spend most of their time waiting.

items.front: What is percent complete and accurate (%C&A)?
items.back: The share of a step's output that the next step can use without corrections.

items.front: ITIL Foundation (Version 5) exam: questions, time and pass mark?
items.back: 40 questions in 60 minutes, closed book. The pass mark is 65%, which is 26 of 40.
